Four sections carry native <h2>; the 480-word Methods section (study site, paired-plot design, coring/assays, mixed-effects stats) is pasted between Introduction and Results with only a bold lead paragraph and NO heading. The Methods block is a substantive, topically-distinct section (per-section obligation of 2.4.10) but its only marker is a font-weight:700

scenario: BOUNDARY PASS variant. Recipe organised into Ingredients / Instructions / Tips & Variations (a genuinely distinct topic). aspectTitle: Visually-demarcated sections (cards, columns, bands, rules, big gaps) with no programmatic heading for each
aspectDescription: The Understanding explicitly warns that 'visual presentation is not sufficient to identify document sections,' yet a very common pattern lays a page out as visually obvious sections — boxed cards, color-banded rows, multi-column blocks, large whitespace gaps, horizontal rules, or tab panels — where each visual block is plainly a distinct section to a sighted user but NONE carries a programmatic heading. The page may have a single page-level h1 (so 047fe0's non-repeated-block check passes) while the several visually-demarcated content sections beneath it use only styled bold leading text, a CSS
scenario: SaaS admin 'Workspace settings' page laid out as four bordered cards (Account, Billing, Notifications, Security). Each card is an unmistakable visual section (box border + tinted header strip + colored dot + 19px/700 bold title), but every card title is a styled <div class="card-title">, not a heading. Section grouping is via <section aria-label> regions only. The single <h1> 'Workspace settings' keeps 047fe0 passing.
mechanism: Four visually-distinct card sections each lack a programmatic heading; the page exposes exactly one heading (the page h1). Screen-reader heading navigation finds only the h1 and cannot jump to the four settings groups. <section aria-label> creates named regions, but regions are a separate mechanism from the section headings 2.4.10 requires.

aspectTitle: Heading element present but its text does not name/introduce its section (wrong, copy-pasted, placeholder, or generic)
aspectDescription: The SC requires headings that 'introduce' their sections and 'clearly indicate the organization of the content' and let users 'know the purpose of each section' — a heading must actually NAME the section it sits above. A page can satisfy the binary presence test while a heading's text is functionally wrong: it describes a DIFFERENT section, was copy-pasted from a template and never updated ('Section Heading', 'Lorem Ipsum'), names the wrong topic (an h2 'Shipping Information' actually heading the returns policy), or is a content-free generic placeholder ('More', 'Stuff', 'Other', 'Untitled') t
scenario: Civic 'Apply for a Residential Parking Permit' page split into three finished, distinct sections (eligibility rules, a fee table, a how-to-apply step list), but all three section h2 read the literal Drupal/CMS template default 'Section Heading' the author never replaced.
mechanism: Mechanism (a) literal CMS placeholder: each section's h2 text is the un-replaced template default 'Section Heading', so the rotor/heading-list reads 'Section Heading' x3 and names none of the sections; the heading is present but introduces no section.

aspectTitle: Multiple distinct navigation/landmark regions, none demarcated by a heading (H69 nav demarcation sub-limb)
aspectDescription: H69 calls for heading markup 'to demarcate different navigational sections like top or main navigation, left or secondary navigation and footer navigation.' Real pages frequently carry several distinct navigation regions — a primary top nav, a secondary/left sidebar nav, in-page section nav, and a footer link nav — yet provide a heading for none of them, so a screen-reader user navigating by heading cannot distinguish 'main navigation' from 'footer navigation' from 'related links.' A human must recognize that the page contains several functionally distinct navigation/grouping regions and judge
scenario: Corporate B2B automation marketing site (Northwind Robotics) with three functionally distinct navigation regions — a top/primary site nav, a left/secondary product sub-category nav, and a footer legal/utility nav — none of which carries a heading; the only heading is the main article h1.
mechanism: Three <nav> landmarks (header.top nav, aside.side nav, footer.foot nav) each begin a functionally distinct navigation section, but none is preceded/labelled by a heading element. A screen-reader user navigating by heading (H key) finds only the single content h1 and cannot distinguish main navigation from product navigation from footer navigation — violating H69's nav-demarcation sub-limb and SC 2.4.10's requirement that each section start with a heading.

aspectTitle: Heading levels contradict the true content hierarchy (a subsection marked as a sibling, or peers given different levels)

aspectTitle: Heading element present and exposed but conveying no section name (whitespace-only, decorative-image-only, CSS-image, or dingbat-only)
aspectDescription: A heading can satisfy the structural presence requirement — an h2 or role=heading element exists, is visible, and is exposed to AT — yet carry no meaningful accessible name for its section: it holds only whitespace / a non-breaking space, only a decorative , only a CSS background-image of the title text with empty real text, or only ornamental glyphs/dingbats. The screen-reader user hears 'heading, level 2' with no label and gains no orientation; the 'mental handle' the SC promises is absent. Whether the rendered heading actually names the section (versus being functionally empty)

A screen-reader heading list announces 'heading, level 2' (or 'blank') with no section name between four named headings, so the user gets no 'mental handle' for the cost/payment section and must read linearly.

aspectTitle: Genuinely unsectioned prose (letter / pre-existing document / continuous narrative) correctly NOT requiring headings
aspectDescription: 2.4.10 is Level AAA precisely because 'it cannot be applied to all types of content and it may not always be possible to insert headings' — posting a pre-existing document whose author included no headings, or a long letter covering several topics where 'putting headings into a letter would be very strange.' Correctly judging that such a page is NOT in scope (the content is genuinely a single flowing document, not 'organized into sections') versus a page that IS sectioned and merely lacks headings requires reading the prose and deciding whether it has the topical structure the SC targets. This
scenario: Family-archive verbatim reproduction of a personal WWII letter (salutation, several topic-shifting paragraphs — crossing, weather, money, brother Tom, food — sign-off, P.S.). The only heading is the archive's catalogue <h1> for the artefact; the letter body has no internal headings. Genre = personal letter, the canonical AAA-inapplicability case.
mechanism: Content is a single continuous personal communication, not 'organized into sections', so 2.4.10's applicability precondition is unmet. Per the Understanding text, 'a long letter would often cover different topics, but putting headings into a letter would be very strange'; and as a pre-existing document, headings the author never wrote 'cannot be inserted'. A screen reader hears one heading (the archive label) and reads the letter as one continuous voice — which is correct. Flagging it for no section headings would be a false positive.
